query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The long‐term structural and chemical stability of multi‐element, near‐equiatomic solid‐solution nanoparticles under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions is governed by the ability to form and maintain a thin, self‐passivating surface layer (e.g., an oxide or carbide) that kinetically restricts surface segregation and sintering. In nanoparticles where the high configurational entropy promotes uniform mixing in the core, the controlled surface passivation acts as a barrier to fast atomic diffusion during service, preserving the single-phase structure.
generation.material_initial_state: As-synthesized, near-equiatomic HEA nanoparticles (e.g., a mix of noble and inexpensive transition metals) with a single-phase, chemically homogeneous solid solution and a high density of surface atoms that are prone to reconstruction under thermal exposure.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled surface treatment—either by an annealing step in a low oxygen partial pressure or by a mild post-synthesis deposition of a thin passivating layer (e.g., a sub-nanometer oxide or carbide formation)—to pre-form the protective surface shell before exposing the nanoparticles to service conditions.
generation.conditions: Testing under catalytic operation conditions at 773–1173 K or thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K; experiments carried out in controlled atmospheres (inert or with a tuned low oxygen partial pressure) over durations relevant to service (hours to tens of hours) with subsequent morphological and compositional characterization.
generation.structural_mediator: A pre-formed, coherent surface passivation layer (of controlled thickness) that minimizes atomic diffusion at the nanoparticle surface, thereby preserving the core’s high-entropy, single-phase structure.
generation.mechanism: The protective surface layer acts by preventing rapid atomic diffusion and surface reconstruction. This barrier limits sintering and phase segregation by kinetically trapping the high-entropy configuration. The high configurational entropy in the core stabilizes the uniform mixing, while the passivation layer prevents externally driven degradation mechanisms at the nanoparticle surface.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to nanoparticles without the controlled surface treatment (baseline), treated nanoparticles will exhibit reduced particle coarsening, lower compositional segregation (as evidenced by minimal change in surface elemental ratios), and preserved phase homogeneity during and after exposure to high-temperature service conditions.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles synthesized by standard methods that have a clean, unmodified surface—prone to rapid sintering and chemical segregation at high service temperatures.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for near-equiatomic HEA compositions with sufficient configurational entropy (typically five or more elements in similar molar ratios) and in service regimes where the temperature and atmosphere do not completely oxidize or otherwise chemically transform the pre-formed passivation layer (i.e., up to ~1173 K catalysis and ~1923 K thermoelectrics, provided the atmosphere is controlled).
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty regarding the exact chemical nature and thickness of the passivation layer that optimally balances protection with minimal interference in catalytic or thermoelectric performance. In addition, the influence of specific alloying elements on the ease of forming such a layer requires further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of near-equiatomic HEA nanoparticles using the colloidal synthesis method. In one set (control), leave the nanoparticle surfaces untreated. In the second set (intervention), apply the controlled surface treatment to induce a thin, pre-formed passivation layer. Subject both sets to identical thermal aging experiments in a controlled atmosphere at 900 K (within the catalytic regime) for a fixed duration (e.g., 10 hours).
measurements: Particle size distribution and morphology via TEM before and after aging.
Surface composition and chemical state analysis using XPS to determine any segregation or oxide layer evolution.
Phase identification using XRD to assess whether a single-phase structure is retained.
Catalytic or thermoelectric performance measurements (activity/selectivity or conductivity/Seebeck coefficient) before and after aging.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles with the pre-formed passivation layer exhibit no statistically significant improvement in maintaining chemical homogeneity, particle size, phase stability, or functional performance compared to the untreated control after aging at 900 K, then the hypothesis that a controlled surface passivation layer is the key mediator for stability would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted much attention in various fields with regard to applications as structural materials, biomaterials, supercapacitors, and catalysts., HEAs comprise mixtures of five or more metallic elements at near equiatomic ratios and form simple single solid-solution phases having lattice structures including face-centered cubic (fcc) and body-centered cubic (bcc)., The high configurational entropy of these alloys stabilizes the solid-solution phase such that this phase appears rather than an intermetallic phase or phase segregation., The severe lattice distortion in these materials that results from differences in the atomic sizes of the constituent elements also causes low atomic diffusivity. The unique synergistic effects resulting from combining multiple elements provide high specific strength, ductility, corrosion resistance, and thermal stability, such that HEAs are unique and fascinating materials. High-entropy oxides (HEOs) have aroused growing interest due to fundamental questions relating to their structure formation, phase stability, and the interplay between configurational disorder and physical and chemical properties. Introducing Fe(II) and Mn(II) into a rocksalt HEO is considered challenging, as theoretical analysis suggests that they are unstable in this structure under ambient conditions. Here, we develop a bottom-up method for synthesizing Mn- and Fe-containing rocksalt HEO (FeO-HEO). We present a comprehensive investigation of its crystal structure and the random cation-site occupancy. We show the improved structural robustness of this FeO-HEO and verify the viability of an oxygen sublattice as a buffer layer. Compositional analysis reveals the valence and spin state of the iron species. We further report the antiferromagnetic order of this FeO-HEO below the transition temperature ~218 K and predict the conditions of phase stability of Mn- and Fe-containing HEOs. Our results provide fresh insights into the design and property tailoring of emerging classes of HEOs. AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) are a class of metal alloys consisting of four or more molar equal or near-equal elements. HEA nanomaterials have garnered significant interest due to their wide range of applications, such as electrocatalysis, welding, and brazing. Their unique multi-principle high-entropy effect allows for the tailoring of the alloy composition to facilitate specific electrochemical reactions. This study focuses on the synthesis of high-purity HEA nanoparticles using the method of femtosecond laser ablation synthesis in liquid. The use of ultrashort energy pulses in femtosecond lasers enables uniform ablation of materials at significantly lower power levels compared to longer pulse or continuous pulse lasers. We investigate how various femtosecond laser parameters affect the morphology, phase, and other characteristics of the synthesized nanoparticles. An innovative aspect of our solution is its ability to rapidly generate multi-component nanoparticles with a high fidelity as the input multi-component target material at a significant yielding rate.
